questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: The Bishop score assesses the favourability of the cervix using all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: The Bishop score grades dilatation, effacement, consistency, position of the cervix and station of the head. A score of 6 or more is favourable; below that, cervical ripening with prostaglandin is used before oxytocin.
questions.reference: DC Dutta Obstetrics 9e, Induction of Labour

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: The agent of choice for cervical ripening in an unfavourable cervix at term is:
questions.concept: Prostaglandins soften and efface the cervix, unlike oxytocin which stimulates contractions without ripening. Misoprostol is cheap and effective but must be used cautiously after previous caesarean because of rupture risk.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: Induction of labour is absolutely contraindicated in:
options: Placenta praevia and classical caesarean scar
questions.concept: Absolute contraindications include placenta praevia, vasa praevia, transverse lie, active genital herpes, cord prolapse, previous classical caesarean or myomectomy entering the cavity, and invasive cervical carcinoma.
questions.reference: DC Dutta Obstetrics 9e, Induction of Labour

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: The prerequisite that must be satisfied before applying outlet forceps is:
options: Fully dilated cervix with an engaged head and known position
questions.concept: Forceps require full dilatation, ruptured membranes, an engaged head with known position, adequate pelvis, empty bladder, anaesthesia and consent. Applying forceps before full dilatation causes cervical tears and fetal injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: Compared with forceps, vacuum extraction is associated with more:
questions.concept: Vacuum causes more cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage and jaundice, while forceps cause more maternal genital tract trauma and facial nerve palsy. Vacuum is contraindicated in face presentation and before 34 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: The commonest indication for primary caesarean section is:
options: Failure to progress or cephalopelvic disproportion
questions.concept: Failure to progress with cephalopelvic disproportion is the commonest primary indication, while previous caesarean is the commonest overall indication once repeat operations are counted. Fetal distress and malpresentation follow.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: The lower segment transverse (Kerr) incision is preferred over the classical incision because it:
options: Has a much lower risk of scar rupture in a subsequent pregnancy
Gives better access to a transverse lie
questions.concept: The lower segment is thin, less vascular and heals with a strong scar, so rupture risk in a later pregnancy is about 0.5% versus 4 to 9% for a classical upper segment incision, which is why vaginal birth after caesarean is possible only with the former.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: Uterine hyperstimulation during oxytocin induction is managed by:
options: Stopping oxytocin, left lateral position, oxygen and a tocolytic such as terbutaline if needed
questions.concept: Hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate abnormality is managed by stopping the infusion, repositioning, oxygen and intravenous fluids, with acute tocolysis if the pattern persists, proceeding to delivery if it does not recover.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: A woman with one previous lower segment caesarean requesting vaginal birth requires:
options: A facility with continuous monitoring and immediate access to caesarean and blood
Prolonged second stage to avoid surgery
questions.concept: Trial of labour after caesarean succeeds in about 70% but carries around 0.5% scar rupture risk, so it needs continuous fetal monitoring in a facility able to perform immediate caesarean. Misoprostol induction is avoided.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.topic: Induction, augmentation & operative obstetrics (forceps, vacuum, LSCS)
questions.stem: Amniotomy accelerates labour but carries the risk of:
questions.concept: Artificial rupture of membranes shortens labour and allows assessment of liquor colour, but risks cord prolapse, especially with a high or unengaged head or malpresentation, and ascending infection with prolonged labour.
questions.reference: DC Dutta Obstetrics 9e, Induction of Labour

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The first sign of puberty in girls is:
questions.concept: Thelarche is the first visible change, followed by pubarche, the growth spurt and finally menarche about 2 to 2.5 years later. Any deviation from this sequence needs endocrine evaluation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Primary amenorrhoea is defined as absence of menstruation by age:
options: 15 years with secondary sexual characteristics, or 13 years without them
questions.concept: Evaluation begins at 15 years if secondary sexual characteristics are present, or at 13 if they are absent, or 3 years after thelarche. Earlier evaluation is warranted with clinical clues such as short stature or virilisation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The commonest cause of primary amenorrhoea is:
options: Gonadal dysgenesis, most often Turner syndrome
questions.concept: Gonadal dysgenesis, typically 45,XO Turner syndrome with streak ovaries, high FSH and short stature, is the commonest cause. Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky) is second and presents with normal secondary characteristics and absent uterus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The commonest cause of secondary amenorrhoea in a sexually active woman is:
questions.concept: Pregnancy must always be excluded first with a urine or serum hCG before any other investigation. Thereafter polycystic ovary syndrome, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease and hypothalamic causes are considered.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea due to:
options: Intrauterine adhesions following vigorous curettage or infection
questions.concept: Intrauterine synechiae obliterate the cavity, giving amenorrhoea or hypomenorrhoea with cyclical pain and infertility despite normal ovulation and a positive progesterone challenge failing to induce bleeding. Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is the treatment.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The PALM-COEIN classification of abnormal uterine bleeding classifies leiomyoma under:
questions.concept: PALM covers structural causes - polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy and hyperplasia - and COEIN the non-structural - coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic and not otherwise classified.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Abnormal Uterine Bleeding

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The investigation of choice to exclude endometrial carcinoma in a woman over 40 with abnormal uterine bleeding is:
options: Endometrial biopsy or dilatation and curettage
questions.concept: Endometrial sampling is mandatory in abnormal bleeding above 40, or younger with risk factors such as obesity, anovulation or tamoxifen. Transvaginal ultrasound assessing endometrial thickness complements but does not replace it.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Abnormal Uterine Bleeding

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The most effective medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman wanting to retain her uterus is:
options: Combined oral contraceptive for 3 months only
questions.concept: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss by 80 to 95% and is the most effective medical option, often avoiding hysterectomy. Tranexamic acid and NSAIDs are effective non-hormonal alternatives.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Abnormal Uterine Bleeding

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Precocious puberty in girls is defined as onset of secondary sexual characteristics before:
questions.concept: Development before 8 years in girls or 9 in boys defines precocious puberty. Central causes are gonadotropin-dependent, most often idiopathic in girls, and are treated with GnRH agonists to preserve final adult height.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: In polycystic ovary syndrome, the Rotterdam criteria require any two of:
options: Oligo-ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology
Raised LH, raised FSH and hirsutism
questions.concept: Two of the three Rotterdam criteria establish the diagnosis after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Weight reduction is first-line, with letrozole preferred for ovulation induction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after:
options: One year of regular unprotected intercourse
questions.concept: Twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse defines infertility, though evaluation begins earlier if the woman is over 35 or there is a known cause such as amenorrhoea, previous pelvic infection or undescended testes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The single commonest identifiable cause of female infertility in India is:
options: Tubal factor, largely from genital tuberculosis and pelvic inflammatory disease
questions.concept: Tubal disease from genital tuberculosis and pelvic inflammatory disease is the leading female cause in India, followed by ovulatory dysfunction. Male factor contributes to about 30 to 40% of couples.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The first-line investigation of the male partner in an infertile couple is:
questions.concept: Semen analysis is the essential first test and should be repeated after 2 to 3 months if abnormal. WHO reference values include volume 1.5 mL or more, concentration 15 million per mL, total motility 40% and normal forms 4%.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Tubal patency is most commonly assessed by:
questions.concept: Hysterosalpingography demonstrates tubal patency and uterine cavity contour and has a mild therapeutic flushing effect; laparoscopy with chromopertubation remains the gold standard and allows treatment of adhesions and endometriosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Ovulation is best confirmed by:
options: A mid-luteal serum progesterone above 3 to 5 ng/mL on day 21
questions.concept: Mid-luteal progesterone is the simplest reliable confirmation of ovulation. Follicular tracking by serial ultrasound documenting collapse of the follicle is more precise, and basal body temperature is unreliable.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The current first-line drug for ovulation induction in polycystic ovary syndrome is:
questions.concept: Letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, gives higher live birth rates than clomiphene in polycystic ovary syndrome with fewer multiple pregnancies and no antioestrogenic effect on the endometrium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection is specifically indicated for:
options: Severe oligospermia or azoospermia requiring surgical sperm retrieval
questions.concept: ICSI injects a single spermatozoon directly into the oocyte and is the treatment for severe male factor infertility, including sperm retrieved by TESA or PESA in obstructive azoospermia. Conventional IVF suffices for tubal factor with normal semen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is characterised by:
options: Ovarian enlargement with third space fluid shift, haemoconcentration and thrombosis risk
questions.concept: Excessive VEGF-mediated capillary permeability after gonadotropin stimulation causes ascites, pleural effusion, haemoconcentration, oliguria and thromboembolism. Risk factors include polycystic ovaries, young age and high oestradiol, and it is prevented by cycle segmentation with a GnRH agonist trigger.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Anti-Mullerian hormone is used in fertility assessment because it:
options: Reflects the ovarian reserve and is relatively cycle-independent
questions.concept: AMH produced by granulosa cells of small follicles correlates with the antral follicle count and predicts ovarian response to stimulation, with the advantage of little variation across the cycle, unlike day-3 FSH.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Under the Indian ART and Surrogacy legislation, commercial surrogacy is:
options: Prohibited, with only altruistic surrogacy permitted for eligible couples
questions.concept: The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021 and the ART (Regulation) Act 2021 prohibit commercial surrogacy, allowing only altruistic surrogacy by a close relative for eligible Indian couples, and mandate registration of ART clinics and banks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The classical triad of symptoms in endometriosis is:
questions.concept: Endometriosis typically causes secondary dysmenorrhoea beginning before menses, deep dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain and infertility. Symptom severity correlates poorly with the extent of disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The commonest site of endometriosis is:
questions.concept: The ovary is the commonest site, forming chocolate cysts (endometriomas). The uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas follow, consistent with retrograde menstruation as the leading aetiological theory.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis is:
questions.concept: Direct laparoscopic visualisation of powder-burn lesions, adhesions and endometriomas with biopsy remains the gold standard. CA-125 may be mildly raised but is non-specific, and imaging detects only endometriomas and deep disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Adenomyosis characteristically presents with:
options: Menorrhagia with dysmenorrhoea in a diffusely bulky tender uterus in a parous woman over 35
questions.concept: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium, giving a symmetrically enlarged tender uterus with heavy painful periods, typically in multiparous women over 35. MRI or transvaginal ultrasound shows myometrial junctional zone thickening.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The definitive treatment of adenomyosis in a woman who has completed her family is:
questions.concept: Because the lesion is diffusely within the myometrium, hysterectomy is definitive. The levonorgestrel intrauterine system, GnRH analogues and uterine artery embolisation are uterus-conserving options for younger women.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Medical management of endometriosis works principally by:
options: Inducing a hypo-oestrogenic or progestogen-dominant state to cause atrophy of ectopic endometrium
questions.concept: Continuous progestogens, combined oral contraceptives, GnRH analogues with add-back therapy and dienogest all suppress ovarian oestrogen or oppose it, causing decidualisation and atrophy of implants. They relieve pain but do not improve fertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Endometriosis affecting the ovary forms a cyst known as:
questions.concept: An endometrioma contains altered thick brown blood resembling melted chocolate, is densely adherent, and its rupture causes intense peritonism. It must be distinguished from a haemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: Deep infiltrating endometriosis of the rectovaginal septum is best assessed by:
options: Magnetic resonance imaging or specialised transvaginal ultrasound
questions.concept: MRI maps depth of infiltration, bowel and ureteric involvement, which is essential for planning multidisciplinary surgery. Laparoscopy alone can underestimate retroperitoneal disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: In a woman with endometriosis-related infertility and minimal disease, the intervention that improves conception is:
options: Laparoscopic ablation or excision of visible lesions
Six months of GnMH analogue therapy
questions.concept: Surgical ablation of minimal to mild disease modestly improves spontaneous conception rates, whereas medical suppression does not improve fertility because it is contraceptive during use. Endometrioma excision before IVF is individualised.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.stem: The commonest gynaecological cause of chronic pelvic pain is:
questions.concept: Endometriosis, chronic pelvic inflammatory disease with adhesions and pelvic congestion syndrome are the leading gynaecological causes, but non-gynaecological causes such as irritable bowel syndrome and interstitial cystitis must also be considered.
questions.reference: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology 17e, Chronic Pelvic Pain
